title: [Chapitre] I. Vers une géométrie des formes (topologiques) : notes manuscrites (05/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: L is a connected 'regular 1-form', a 1-dimensional object in Grothendieck's 1986 'géométrie des formes'. It is covered by oriented segments I, each with an origin or(I). On the previous page he showed that the relation it induces is a genuine order, and he set out to prove that this order is strictly filtrant increasing: for all x, y in L there is z with x, z < ... more precisely, with x < z and y < z.

This page gives the attempted proof.
(1) Connectedness gives a chain x=x_0, x_1, ..., x_n=y in which x_i and x_{i+1} both lie in the interior of a segment I_i.
(2) Put y_i = or(I_i). Then x_i >= y_i <= x_{i+1} >= y_{i+1} <= ..., so any two points are joined by a zigzag of inequalities. In other words, L is a zigzag-connected (quasi-)ordered set.
(3) Induction on the length n of the zigzag.
- Base case, length <= 1, say x <= y: it suffices to have some z > y. This follows from regularity (no maximal elements).
- Inductive step: write x ~_{n-1} z ~_1 y. By induction there is x' with x, z < x'.
  - If z >= y, then x' > x, y and we are done.
  - If z <= y, the page breaks off.
(4) The next page reduces this remaining case to a 'filtration relative' (cospan completion) property: if u <= v and u <= w, then there is t >= v, w. Here u = z, v = x', w = y.
(5) The next page then recognises the problem. An order that is locally strictly increasing and decreasing, with no extremal elements, already satisfies the axioms F1–F5 of a connected regular form. But such an order need not be filtrant increasing, nor (dually) decreasing.

So the page is an induction showing that global upward directedness of a zigzag-connected poset reduces to upward amalgamation of 'V' configurations. That amalgamation fails for branching (non-Hausdorff) 1-dimensional objects.
errors: The inductive step in the case z <= y needs the property 'u <= v, u <= w implies a common upper bound of v and w'. This does not follow from the stated axioms (regularity, local filtrations of intervals).

Counterexample: the 'line with a branching', i.e. two copies of R glued along (-inf,0]. With 0 < x in one branch and 0 < y in the other, x and y have no common upper bound. So the intended claim (str. filtrante croissante) is false without a separation/Hausdorff-type hypothesis.
Grothendieck himself notices this on the next page ('une telle structure n'est pas nécessairement filtrante croissante').

ideas.what: Turning connectedness via a chain of overlapping oriented segments into a zigzag of order inequalities through the segment origins
ideas.modern_name: zigzag-connectedness of a poset; connected components of a category/poset

ideas.what: Reducing global upward directedness of a connected poset to an amalgamation property for V-shaped configurations (u<v, u<w implies v,w have an upper bound)
ideas.modern_name: directedness from local amalgamation; Ore-type / cofiltered-category condition
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore (Ore condition; filtered categories in SGA4 / Artin–Grothendieck)
ideas.where_published: Filtered-category conditions appear in SGA4 Exposé I, but not this poset argument

ideas.what: Implicitly: 1-dimensional 'forms' given by locally linear orders may branch, so they behave like non-Hausdorff 1-manifolds / order-trees
ideas.modern_name: non-Hausdorff 1-manifolds, R-order trees (leaf spaces of foliations)

missed.claim: The obstruction found here (locally linear, locally filtrant orders that are not globally directed) is exactly the branching phenomenon behind the Haefliger–Reeb classification of simply connected non-Hausdorff 1-manifolds by order-trees. These notes do not connect it to that theory.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is minor. A combinatorial axiomatics of 1-dimensional 'forms' via orders would naturally include branching 1-manifolds and leaf spaces. That is already known in foliation theory, so the novelty is small.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine order-theoretic induction that is left incomplete, and the intended claim is false in general; the following page acknowledges this. The only point of interest is the implicit encounter with branching (non-Hausdorff) 1-dimensional structures, which are well known.
